Inside the insurance industry’s destruction lab
November 6, 2026 • When you think of someone burning down a house for insurance purposes, you don’t imagine it would ever be the insurance company itself lighting the match. But that’s essentially what’s happening inside a giant destruction laboratory, funded by the insurance industry, in the woods of South Carolina. Scientists and engineers there build household structures — from decks to sheds to single family homes — and subject them to literal trials by fire, hail, and hurricane force wind. It’s all in hopes of determining which building materials and techniques will make communities across the country more resilient to natural disasters and make those natural disasters less expensive for insurance companies.

U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October as the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. The warehouse and transportation industry added 25,000 jobs during the month.
Scott Olson/Getty Images North America
hide caption
Scott Olson/Getty Images North America
The U.S. job market picked up steam last month.
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, according to a report Friday from the Labor Department. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%, from 4.2% the previous month.
Employment gains for August and September were revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs.
Industries adding jobs last month include health care, manufacturing, and business services. Meanwhile, restaurants and construction companies cut jobs during the month.
One sign of the strengthening job market was slightly larger wage gains. Average wages in October were up 3.1% from a year ago. That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month, but still probably not enough to keep pace with rising prices.
Inflation climbed to 3.7% in September. The cost of living has been going up faster than wages for much of this year, since the war with Iran triggered a sharp jump in energy prices.
"Workers are losing ground right now," says Cory Stahle, an economist with the Indeed job-search website. "The longer it wears on, the more and more they're going to feel that."
Voters' frustration with high prices was a big factor in the midterm elections, which cost Republicans their majorities in both the House and Senate.
The unemployment rate remains historically low, which has allowed the Federal Reserve to focus its attention on fighting inflation. The central bank held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, but investors expect the Fed to raise rates when policymakers meet in December.

Cooper Katz McKim
You're reading a newsletter from  The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter.  Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
Scammers can even make money off of people starved for FAN fiction. That's my takeaway from a fake website popping up that tried to sell computer-generated audiobooks of fan fiction, which is content created by ANYONE based off of existing works. "Fifty Shades of Grey" started as a fanfic of Twilight, for example.
This scam website popped up in the wake of the uber-popular fan fiction website AO3, Archive of our Own, going down for an estimated two to four weeks after a "security incident." People are starved for their stories and apparently will click on anything. Lucky for the world, the scam website has been taken down.
Coming up
How criminals are racing to launder stolen crypto
Why gold prices are at a one-year low
The origin of fear around the adjustable-rate mortgage
News We're Watching
How to launder THAT much cryptocurrency
What to know: North Korea just loves stealing crypto. They love it! It's become a major part of their economy. Last week, a state-sponsored hacking group called "TraderTraitor" executed the largest crypto theft in history, stealing $6.43 billion from Binance, a massive cryptocurrency exchange. $2.85 billion has been frozen or seized, according to Elliptic, a crypto analytics & compliance firm. But $3.35 billion is still linked to the group. "TraderTraitor" is actively trying to launder this money (yes, crypto is surprisingly traceable). A huge part of the stolen funds are in stablecoin, which can be frozen. Whatever isn't already frozen, the hacking group is trying to launder it and FAST. So how are they doing it?
"TraderTraitor" is trying to quickly turn Stablecoin into Ether, a harder to freeze crypto
PETER PARKS/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
hide caption
PETER PARKS/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
How are the criminals laundering these assets?: Laundering this much crypto is NOT simple. The intelligence firm Elliptic broke down how "TraderTraitor" is trying to quickly protect its newfound loot. First of all, they want to turn any Stablecoin into assets that cannot be frozen, like Ether (ETH). From there, the group is using automation to create LOTS of new wallets to filter small amounts of crypto, so as not to trigger alarms for moving assets worth a bazillion dollars. From there, launderers want to move the money across networks like Ethereum to Bitcoin then pull it from a mixed pool with a bunch of other people's assets. The goal: make the crypto's origins hazy. "TraderTraitor" is moving fast. On Tuesday, Elliptic reported the group has made more than 40,000 transactions, creating a new wallet every 25 seconds.
One interesting detail: Binance has promised to make customers whole, but investors have already pulled billions from the exchange.
Why gold prices are being weird
What to know: This week, gold fell below $4,000 per ounce after hitting nearly $5,600 per ounce in January. It's typically seen as a safe-haven asset, which is why investors were shoveling money into it earlier this year. As you know, things have been a bit volatile from the Iran War to the criminal probe into the Federal Reserve chair. But today, there's still economic uncertainty, no? The war with Iran rages on. So why are gold prices falling? I took my question to Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo to find out. I asked him: could gold be going down because Treasury bond yields are up? That could mean there are MORE reliable ways to make money.
Why is gold going down?: Our answer, courtesy of Jeff Guo!
Jeff: I think you are right that rising Treasury yields are the story. As you know, gold tends to be seen as a "safe" asset and an inflation hedge; but the problem is that gold doesn't earn any income/interest on its own. Meanwhile, you could buy a 10 year TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) bond right now that does earn income, above and beyond inflation. Sure, the Iran war is a source of political instability that might drive investors toward gold. But the main effect of the war so far seems to be raising the price of oil. And higher oil prices are one of the factors pushing interest rates up, making bonds more attractive relative to gold.
THANK YOU JEFF!
What the election means for data centers - Washington Post
What to know: People do not want data centers and the election left us with numbers to prove it. Apparently voters either BANNED or placed restrictions on data centers in at least 38 jurisdictions across the country. The numbers within the ballot measures were fascinating. It's also notable that Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, ran on a platform of reining in data centers. She called for a moratorium on new projects and pushing for more aggressive protections on both ratepayers and the environment. A Democrat hasn't been governor in Texas in more than 30 years.
Why it matters: All this local opposition could actually make an impact on what big tech wants to do. Local opposition has already made a difference in data center world. S&P Global has tracked projects nationwide and found more than 146 were delayed or canceled through early August. 75% of those were tied to local opposition. articles.title: Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks
articles.text:
Stocks sink as AI fears build after midterms : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Stocks sink as AI fears build after midterms Shares sank, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropping over 5%, as investors reacted with fear that a Democratic Congress — and states across the country -— would crack down on AI and data centers.
Business
Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks
November 5, 20267:16 PM ET
By
Rafael Nam
AI shares sink after blue wave
Listen
3:46
3:46
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6031987/nx-s1-9993987" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
Stocks sank as investors fear an incoming Democratic Congress — and states across the country — could crack down on the AI industry and data centers.
Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images
Two days after Democrats won overwhelmingly in the national midterm elections — and in state races across the country — investors started to come to terms with the potential consequences.
Elections
6 takeaways from Democrats' big wave on election night
Fears that an incoming Democratic Congress would crack down on AI sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq down more than 5% and wiped out more than $2 trillion in market value. The Dow Jones and S&P also sank.
The losses were a stark reversal from Wednesday, when investors had initially sent shares higher across the board, relieved that the midterms did not end with the fate of Congress undecided.
Politics
How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
The sobering-up seen across markets on Thursday reflected investors' concern about a big signal sent by voters: They revolted against AI data centers, which many people worry will gobble up water and energy resources. Those voters supported Democrats who have vowed to push back against the proliferation of these projects.
But many AI companies — including Meta and Alphabet, the parent company of Google — need to keep building out these data centers to continue developing the technology.
The Nasdaq's decline comes after what has already been a rough year of technology shares on Wall Street, with investors starting to question whether the massive investments companies have plowed into AI will pay off anytime soon.
"There is some concern regarding AI regulation, and fears that there could be far more regulations coming to AI technology, as well as a pushback on the buildout of data centers across the country," says David Busch, chief investment officer of Trajan Wealth.
Musk companies hit hard
AI-related or AI-dependent stocks of all kinds were among the biggest decliners on Thursday, with Tesla and SpaceX — both controlled by billionaire Elon Musk — falling particularly sharply. Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars in an unsuccessful attempt to elect more Republicans, and investors fear he and his companies could also come under Democratic scrutiny when the new Congress is seated in January.
Only on NPR
The South flexes political power in midterms, sets regional influence in 2028 election
It's not only Congress, however. Democrats who vowed to slow down AI development also won at the state level, most prominently Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governor's race in stunning fashion.
It's unclear whether the AI stock rout will continue — or spread beyond tech stocks. AI has become a big driver of the U.S. economy, helping it post a solid annual growth of 3.4% in the July-September quarter.
And sophisticated Wall Street investors are not the only ones who own a lot of shares in AI companies. Average Americans also own them through their retirement investment portfolios — such as 401(k)s or pension funds — leaving them also vulnerable to a prolonged AI rout.

articles.title: First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
articles.text:
Record share of first-time homebuyers pay all cash : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Record share of first-time homebuyers pay all cash A new report finds generational wealth is widening the divide between homebuyers and those priced out. The median age of first-time buyers also remains at a record high.
Housing
First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
November 5, 202610:00 AM ET
Heard on Morning Edition
Jennifer Ludden
First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
Listen
2:30
2:30
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6022491/nx-s1-9994349" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
A "for sale" sign is posted in front of a home on July 09, 2026 in Los Angeles, Calif. A new report finds generational wealth is helping a record share of first-time homebuyers pay with all cash.
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
hide caption
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.
"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.
First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.
NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.
Affordability
How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."
The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."
Your Money
Here's the latest sticker shock: Borrowing for a mortgage — or a car
Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.
"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.
But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.
High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth. Miller sees more clients getting help from family members who may have paid off their own home, or have equity in a second property they can sell and "are gifting some or all of that money." They're viewing it as a kind of "future inheritance," he said.
For some younger first-time buyers, relatives may only be "lending them the cash" to make a bid more attractive, said Nate Johnson, a broker associate with RedKey Realty Leaders in St. Louis. Even with much of the national housing market in a major slump, he said his local market is still intensely competitive for buyers.
Economy
It's getting harder to afford rent in the U.S., even for middle-income families
"They just know that if we're looking at five or six offers on the table, let's call it 10 offers on the table, which is not uncommon…maybe three of those offers will be all cash," he said.
After closing on a property, Johnson has seen some buyers refinance into a mortgage and pay back their family member.
The rise of all-cash offers makes the market even tougher for those who struggle to save up for a down payment with today's sky-high home prices.
"For a long time I thought I wanted to buy a house," said Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33. They and their spouse have good jobs, but also debt, including a car payment and student loans. Not only does Esmeson think they may never be in a position to buy, they've also decided it does not make sense at today's prices.
Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33, has decided to put off buying a home, in part due to debts like a car payment and student loans.
Jane Corbit
hide caption
Jane Corbit
"Being that debt burdened, and also having to fix things on your home, like, it sounds really terrible," they said.
Esmeson is also not convinced that home equity would outpace other investments. They like their current rental and landlord so are sticking with it for now.
Still, it's frustrating that the housing market worked better for previous generations. "We have the short end of the deal," they said, and "the gap is expanding."
There's probably only one way they might ever be able to buy. "If I received an inheritance," they said. But "I love my mom dearly and I don't want to look forward to that, or really want to strategize around that."

articles.title: As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
articles.text:
People are breaking out their library cards to save money : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
People are breaking out their library cards to save money Some Americans squeezed by high prices are relying more on their local libraries for things like books, streaming services and high-priced items like musical instruments and sewing machines.
Economy
As budgets tighten, people are breaking out their library cards
November 5, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Joe Hernandez
People study in the Rose Main Reading Room of the New York Public Library in midtown Manhattan on July 06, 2021.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
hide caption
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Izzy Rivera reads at least one book every week, but buying them new isn't in her budget. As she saves up for law school, some expenses don't make the cut.
"Say I'm buying a few a month," she said, "it just isn't realistic."
That's why Rivera has recently been leaning more on local libraries near her home in Topeka, Kan., checking out both physical books and digital copies on the Libby app. (Some of her recent reads: Sour Cherry by Natalia Theodoridou, Spoilt Creatures by Amy Twigg and Plastic Inc. by Beth Gardiner.) Rivera also went to her library's used book sale last month, where she picked up 15 books for about $20.
The library's money-saving potential doesn't end there for her. Rivera also watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, reads the New York Times at no cost and often passes the time at a local branch.
Business
This is how close American households are to the financial edge
"It's somewhere I can go where I'm not expected to spend money," she said. "If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn't want a coffee."
It is something of a truism in the library world that, when economic conditions worsen, people use libraries more. Patrons and librarians across the U.S. tell NPR they're seeing that pan out now.
Prices for food and other everyday items continue to rise in part because of the war with Iran, and affordability was a top concern among voters heading into the midterm elections. According to a Pew Research Center survey released in mid-October, 44% of Americans say they've struggled in the past year to afford at least one basic necessity, such as medical care or their rent or mortgage payment. Seventy percent of adults also said they've cut back on "extras," such as subscriptions to streaming services.
Data shared with NPR by several of the largest public library systems in the U.S. show recent upticks in cardholder membership, circulation and event attendance. Librarians say part of that can be attributed to the rising cost of living — and the growing recognition that libraries' resources extend far beyond physical books.
Life Kit
How the local library can save you money
"People start off with Audible and then a friend tells them, 'Why are you paying for that? You can get that at the library if you're a smidgen bit patient,'" said Jeremy Reeder, director of the Maricopa County Library District in Arizona.
Of course, the rising cost of living is not the only factor driving more people to check out libraries. Many institutions have gotten better at marketing themselves, librarians say, and social media has helped foster a renewed cultural interest in reading.
"Libraries have been popular for a really long time, but I think that there's heightened awareness of the wide range of offerings that our libraries are providing," said Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association. "They are especially popular right now, I think, because people are aware that everything that we provide is free or very low cost."
By the numbers
There is historical precedent for the idea that economic slumps are a boon to libraries.
An analysis by the American Library Association found that circulation increased at 18 large public library systems during a brief U.S. recession in 2001. Another study of 541 libraries found that library use was higher during the Great Recession than in previous years. (However, a 1986 article that tried to draw a similar correlation found no data to support that theory.)
Business
The economic squeeze is pushing up poverty rates for older adults
Though it's unclear to what extent affordability concerns are pushing people to libraries now, several large public systems have reported growth in recent years.
Usage of the Los Angeles Public Library's makerspace grew 37% between the last two fiscal years, while digital circulation and library visits were both up over 20%. In-person visits, adult library card applications and Wi-Fi sessions at the Chicago Public Library all jumped by more than 11% year-over-year from January through July. The Maricopa County Library District, which has seen its cardholder base grow sharply as it moved its application process online, recorded a 34% increase in Kanopy use and a 78% surge in Hoopla use over the past three years.
The Topeka and Shawnee County Public Library, where Izzy Rivera goes, logged an 8.1% increase in digital media checkouts last year, though physical circulation is down. There's also been a surge in requests for tech support, such as help with online job applications.
OverDrive, the company that owns Kanopy, reported a 41% spike in users of the streaming service last year alone.
The landscape for libraries
In general, libraries are on a cultural come-up: They're increasingly popular among Gen Z and Millennials — even those who aren't big readers. And there's more interest in reading writ large, as social media phenomena such as #BookTok fuel book sales.
Another change in library use began during the pandemic, when lockdowns forced users to acclimate to digital media, such as the e-books and streaming apps offered by libraries. "It was already a trend pre-pandemic," said Los Angeles Public Library senior librarian Edwin Rodarte, "but th

articles.title: Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don't hold your breath
articles.text:
Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don’t hold your breath : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don’t hold your breath A new Democratic majority in Congress could pressure the president to end the war in Iran. But it will be harder for them to directly affect fuel prices, which are tied to a complex international oil market.
Business
Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don't hold your breath
November 5, 20265:00 AM ET
Heard on Morning Edition
Willa Rubin
Does the blue wave mean lower gasoline and diesel prices soon? Don’t hold your breath
Listen
4:02
4:02
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6029365/nx-s1-9994320" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
A customer replaces the nozzle on a gasoline pump after making a purchase at Fuel City filling station Friday, April 17, 2026, in Dallas.
Tony Gutierrez/AP
hide caption
Tony Gutierrez/AP
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
Democrats are now poised to take control of Congress by wide margins — and a critical driver of their success has been voter fury about how the war in Iran has driven up the cost of fuel.
Before the war, about one fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. As the war throttled that waterway, the price of oil rose: A barrel of Brent crude cost about $70 in late February, spent months hovering around the $110 mark, and is now close to $95.
That's driven up the price of everything that's refined from crude. A gallon of gas costs $4.12 on average — about $1 higher than a year ago. The price of diesel hit a record high in September at $6.52, and while it's fallen a bit since then, a gallon remains about $2.50 higher than this time last year, according to AAA.
Business
Oil company earnings skyrocket — again
Business
Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
These soaring prices helped major oil companies rake in huge profits over the past two quarters, while making the cost of fuel at the pump uncomfortably high for drivers, and boosting the price of nearly everything in a nation that is heavily reliant on trucking.
So now that the midterm results are in, could drivers see lower gasoline and diesel prices anytime soon?
Not so fast, experts say. Here's why.
What could Democrats do?
Nothing yet — members of the new Congress won't be sworn in until January.
Middle East conflict
Why it's so hard for world leaders to bring down oil and gasoline prices
Business
Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel
And once they are seated, U.S. legislators have limited powers to directly affect the price of oil, which is dictated by a complex global market.
In the run-up to the election, most of the actions taken by the federal government to lower fuel prices came through the White House, not Congress. Hoping to stave off losses for his party, President Trump tried to ease the cost of diesel by loosening federal rules on dyed diesel, which is normally used for farming. He also announced a deal that would bring more Russian diesel to global markets, including the U.S., by temporarily lifting sanctions. Neither of these did much to move the needle.
But the new Congressional Democrats will have the power to push the president to end the war in Iran, in part by making it harder to authorize new war spending. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D.-NY) told reporters on Wednesday that Democrats are intent on ending the war and bringing down the cost of living, saying that "relief is on the way."
"What a unified Democratic Congress can do is make escalation considerably more costly: both chambers can pass resolutions, attach conditions to war spending and hold back confirmations of key officials," Claudio Galimberti, chief economist of Rystad Energy, wrote in a market note to the media.
Business
The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars
Still, the president has veto power over legislation, as well as executive powers. " President Trump still retains full discretionary authority over military strikes, over blockades and sanctions, licenses, and so on," said Jorge León,  head of geopolitical analysis at Rystad Energy, in an interview with NPR.
Trump has sent mixed messages about whether he wants to end or escalate the war. In the past few weeks, he warned Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a new military campaign after the midterms. The U.S. struck Qeshm, an island in the Strait of Hormuz that Iran uses to launch its own strikes, on Nov. 2.
But on election night, Trump told The New York Times that he knew voters were unhappy about gas prices. And the next day, as the extent of the election rout became clear, Vice President JD Vance posted on social media: "The reason we lost is the war."
If the war ends, when would prices fall?
Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, says if there's a deal to end the war, traders could be very excited. Brito said they might look for formal announcements from both Iran and the U.S. that the strait is reopening, and that both sides are pulling back their military presence in the area.
Business
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is low. Here's why you should care
If market traders are convinced the peace will last? "If that scenario happens, then I personally see crude prices dropping, you know, $15, $20 [a barrel] immediately, in the next two, three days from the announcement," he said.
But for gasoline and diesel prices to fall, too, oil would have to start moving again. Ships that have been running long, alternative routes to avoid passing through the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, and then resume their former routes through the strait. León poi
